THE SAVOY MALE AND FEMALE COLLEGE  77

On special occasions—such as holidays, end-of-school exhibitions, and trips with the debating teams to neighboring colleges—the rules were suspended, and social activity moved in an exciting whirl. These occasions were matters of high interest because the rules, strict as they were, were respected and abided by rather minutely throughout the school, and most of the students were serious-minded enough not to resent the repression. The high moral standards were kept up by wholesome precept and example on the part of the faculty, and many students remember the strong impress of the characters of the faculty members. A personal letter to the writer from Mr. T. P. Wells sums up the tenor of many conversations with ex-students:

      One of the outstanding characteristics of Savoy College students was that they left the school filled with worthy and noble ambition. As a result of this many became men and women of distinction and useful to the world in many walks of life.
      There was no athletics taught in the school. The burning desire was to burn the "mid-night oil" and become a scholar. The moral training was of a higher standard than it is in colleges today.⁶³

⁶³Personal letter from Mr. T. P. Wells, Bells, Texas, July 12, 1938.
